title: What If We Drew Again? Sample Means from a Skewed Population

steps.instruction: The **Population** panel shows a strongly **right-skewed** population — most values sit low, with a few large values stretching a long tail to the right. Its true mean **μ** is marked. We can't see a whole population in real life, but here we can. We'll draw samples of **n = 10** and track the **mean** \(\bar{x}^*\) of each sample.
steps.observe: Find **μ** marked on the Population panel. A single sample of 10 values will rarely have a mean exactly equal to μ — that sample-to-sample wobble is what we're about to study.

steps.instruction: **Before you draw anything, commit to a prediction.** In the chapter, samples of runners gave proportions that piled up at the population's proportion. Now imagine taking *hundreds* of samples of n = 10 from this skewed population and plotting each sample's mean \(\bar{x}\).

gate.question: The population is right-skewed. Where will those sample means (\(\bar{x}\)) pile up?

choices.text: Centered around μ, the population mean
choices.feedback: You've committed — now draw samples and watch where the center of the pile actually lands.

choices.text: Pulled to the right of μ, toward the long tail
choices.feedback: You've committed — the skew is tempting. Draw samples and check where the center really falls.
You've committed — draw and see whether the means spread out evenly or cluster somewhere.

steps.instruction: Click **+1** once. The **One sample** panel shows your 10 drawn values; they collapse to a single **mean** \(\bar{x}^*\), which drops as one dot into the **Sampling distribution** panel at the bottom. Click **+1** a few more times.

requires.hint: Click **+1** a few times (at least 5 draws), then continue.

steps.observe: Each dot is **one sample's mean** — not one observation. The \(\bar{x}\)'s bounce around from sample to sample, but where do they seem to gather?

steps.instruction: Now click **+1000** to draw a thousand samples quickly and let the sampling distribution fill in.

requires.hint: Click **+1000** to draw at least 500 sample means, then answer below.

steps.observe: Look at the **Sampling distribution** panel and its **SD of \(\bar{x}\)'s** readout: the typical distance of a sample mean from μ. The chapter calls that SD the **standard error**.

gate.question: Even though the population is strongly right-skewed, where is the distribution of \(\bar{x}\) centered, and how does its shape compare to the population?

choices.text: Centered at μ, and less skewed (more symmetric) than the population
Centered to the right of μ, and just as skewed as the population

gate.feedback: It centers at **μ**, and averaging just 10 values already pulls the shape toward symmetric: the skew is fading. Your **{{samples}}** sample means have an SD of **{{statSD}}**: that is how far a sample mean typically lands from μ. Watch what happens to the shape, and to that SD, when you increase n next.
gate.retryFeedback: Look at where the dots pile up relative to the μ line, and compare the shape of the **Sampling distribution** panel to the skewed **Population** panel.

steps.instruction: Two different changes affect this picture in two different ways. First click **+1000 again** (more samples, same n = 10). Then click **Freeze this distribution to compare**, change **Sample size (n) to 100**, and draw **+1000** — so you see both at once.

requires.hint: Freeze the n = 10 distribution, set **Sample size (n)** to **100**, and draw **+1000**.

steps.observe: Compare the frozen n = 10 distribution to the new n = 100 one, and watch the **SD of \(\bar{x}\)'s** readout drop.

gate.question: Which change made the sampling distribution **narrower** — and which just filled it in more smoothly?

choices.text: Increasing the sample size to n = 100 narrowed it

gate.feedback: Only a larger **n** narrows it. More samples (more dots) just fill in the *same* n = 10 distribution more smoothly; its spread doesn't change. A larger n produces a *different*, narrower distribution, because each mean now averages over more values, so the highs and lows cancel more. The SD readout at n = 100 is about a third of the one at n = 10. And the n = 100 distribution is close to bell-shaped, while the center stayed at μ the whole time.
gate.retryFeedback: Compare the frozen n = 10 distribution to the n = 100 one — same center at μ, different width. Then recall what adding more dots at n = 10 did to the width.

steps.instruction: You've built the sampling distribution of a sample mean from scratch — starting from a skewed population. Before you read the summary, put the key ideas in your own words.

prompts.label: Why does the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) end up centered at μ, even though the population's long tail is all on the right?
Why does a larger n shrink the spread, when drawing more samples doesn't?

respond.answer: A strong answer: averaging has no built-in lean, so over many samples the means that come out too high balance the ones that come out too low, and the pile sits at μ. A big value from the tail gets averaged with ordinary ones, so it can't drag a mean far. A larger n shrinks the spread because each mean rests on more values, so more of the highs and lows cancel. Drawing more samples only shows the same distribution in more detail.

steps.reveal: The sample mean \(\bar{x}\) varies from sample to sample, but predictably: its distribution is **centered at the population mean μ**, it **narrows as n grows**, and it becomes close to **bell-shaped** as n grows, even when the population itself is skewed. **More samples** sharpen the picture of that distribution; a **larger n** changes it. Its standard deviation, the **standard error**, is how far a sample mean typically lands from μ. Why the shape turns bell-shaped, and a shortcut for the spread, come at the end of the unit.
